source_text: XII. Haec omnes de carcere simul scripserant, sed quia necesse erat omnem actum martyrum beatorum pleno sermone complecti, quia et ipsi de se per modestiam minus dixerant et Flavianus quoque privatim hoc nobis munus iniunxit, ut quicquid litteris eorum deesset adderemus, necessaria reliqua subiunximus. cum per plurimos menses reclusi tulissent carceris poenas et fame et siti diu laborassent, tandem sero produci iubentur et ad praetorium praesidis admoveri. et omnibus quidem gloriosa voce confessis, cum Flaviani adiutorium reclamaret amore perverso, negans eum diaconum, quod confitebatur in ceteros, id est Lucium, Montanum, Iulianum, Victoricum, dicta sententia est, Flavianusque rursum receptus est. et quamvis haberet plenam doloris materiam, quia scilicet de tam bono collegio separatus est, tamen fide et devotione qua vixit credebat: id fieri quod deus vellet, et tristitiam solitudinis destitutae religio sapientiae temperabat. dicebat etiam: Cum cor regis in manu dei sit, quae causa moeroris est, aut quare succensendum putem homini, qui hoc loquitur quod iubetur? sed de Flaviano postmodum plenius.
thought_title: Sentence pronounced and Flavian kept back
orientation: The prisoners letter has ended and an editor now adds what happened after long imprisonment.
pass_a_gloss: These things all together had written from prison, but because it was necessary to embrace every act of the blessed martyrs with a full account, and because they themselves concerning themselves through modesty had said less and Flavian also privately imposed this task upon us, that whatever was lacking to their letters we should add, we have added below the remaining necessary things. When shut up through very many months they had borne the punishments of prison and with hunger and thirst for a long time had suffered, at last late they are ordered to be led out and to be brought to the court of the governor. And with all indeed having given testimony with a glorious voice, when the assistant of Flavian was crying out against it with perverse love, denying him to be deacon, which he was declaring against the rest, that is against Lucius, Montanus, Julian, Victoricus, sentence was pronounced, and Flavian was received back again. And although he had full matter of grief, because evidently he had been separated from so good a company, nevertheless by the faith and devotion by which he lived he was believing: that to be happening which God wished, and the sadness of abandoned solitude the religion of wisdom was tempering. He was saying also: Since the heart of the king is in the hand of God, what cause of grief is there, or why should I think that anger must be felt toward the man, who speaks this which he is ordered to speak? But concerning Flavian more fully afterwards.

bible_refs.note: Cum cor regis in manu dei sit

pass_b_english: They all wrote this together from prison. But the whole record of the blessed martyrs had to be set out fully. They themselves had said too little about themselves out of modesty, and Flavian had also laid this task on us in private, to add whatever was missing from their letter. So we have added below the rest that was needed.

They had been shut up for many months and had borne the pains of prison, suffering hunger and thirst for a long time. Then at last, late in the day, they were ordered to be led out and brought to the governor's court. All of them gave testimony with a glorious voice. But Flavian's assistant protested out of a perverse love, denying that Flavian was a deacon, though he made the same testimony as the others, that is Lucius, Montanus, Julian, and Victoricus. Sentence was pronounced, and Flavian was received back again.

Flavian had every reason for grief, since he had been separated from so good a company. Yet in the faith and devotion he had lived by, he believed that what was happening was what God willed, and wise devotion tempered the sorrow of his lonely abandonment. As he put it, "The king's heart is in the hand of God (Proverbs 21:1), so what reason is there for grief, or why should I be angry with a man who says only what he is commanded to say?" But we will tell more about Flavian later.
notes: uncertainty in the Flavian clause: relation of negans eum diaconum to quod confitebatur in ceteros is syntactically strained; gloss keeps source order without resolving role of adiutorium

problems.quote: while giving testimony against the others
problems.why: The Latin says the assistant denied Flavian was a deacon even though Flavian shared the testimony given for the others. 'Against the others' turns the confession into hostile testimony, which the source does not say.
problems.fix: denying that Flavian was a deacon, though he made the same testimony as the others, that is Lucius, Montanus, Julian, and Victoricus.
problems.ruling: 'confitebatur' means confess/profess, not testify against; 'in ceteros' means regarding others, so 'against' misleads reader.

edits.old: denying that Flavian was a deacon while giving testimony against the others, that is Lucius, Montanus, Julian, and Victoricus
edits.new: denying that Flavian was a deacon, though he made the same testimony as the others, that is Lucius, Montanus, Julian, and Victoricus

fixed: Fixed hostile 'against the others': quod confitebatur in ceteros has Flavian sharing the testimony of the rest, not testifying against them.
